en: Mount Pinatubo's massive 1991 eruption was the second-largest volcanic event of the 20th century and temporarily cooled the global climate.
The Puerto Princesa Subterranean River in Palawan features an underground river that flows directly into the sea, experiencing tidal influences.
The Philippine Sea contains the Philippine Trench, which features the Galathea Depth, one of the deepest oceanic points on Earth.
The Sierra Madre mountain range acts as a natural shield, protecting Luzon from the strongest typhoons coming from the Pacific Ocean.
The island of Palawan is home to the Philippine mouse-deer, which is recognized as one of the smallest hoofed mammals in the world.
The Philippines is the world's top producer of abaca, a natural fiber native to the country used for making strong ropes.
The Pagsanjan River in Laguna features dramatic rapids and waterfalls that require skilled local boatmen to navigate using small, traditional wooden boats.
Mount Mayon in Albay is globally renowned for possessing the most perfectly symmetrical volcanic cone shape among all active volcanoes.
Situated directly within the Pacific Typhoon Belt, the Philippine archipelago experiences an average of 20 tropical cyclones every single year.
Lake Taal in Batangas is a unique freshwater lake that completely encloses Volcano Island, which itself contains a smaller crater lake.
The Banaue Rice Terraces in Ifugao were carved into the steep Cordillera mountains over 2,000 years ago using basic hand tools.
Tubbataha Reefs in the Sulu Sea is a UNESCO World Heritage site that serves as a massive, protected sanctuary for thousands of marine species.
